headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Amenorrhoea
headings.content: Amenorrhoea is defined as the absence of menstruation in a woman of reproductive age. It is not a disease in itself, but rather a clinical sign of an underlying physiological abnormality or pathological condition. Understanding this condition is crucial for nursing students preparing for clinical practice and exams in Nigeria, as menstrual irregularities are frequently encountered in gynaecological settings. Amenorrhoea can be a temporary state, such as during pregnancy or lactation, or it can indicate serious endocrine, anatomical, or genetic disorders. Clinically, it is categorized into two main types: primary and secondary amenorrhoea. Recognising the distinction helps nurses perform thorough assessments, provide appropriate health education, and guide patients toward timely diagnostic evaluations. Proper identification of amenorrhoea ensures that conditions affecting fertility, bone health, and overall endocrine balance are managed effectively. Nurses play a frontline role in taking detailed menstrual histories, supporting patients through emotional distress, and collaborating with multidisciplinary healthcare teams to restore normal reproductive health.

headings.title: Physiology of Normal Menstruation and the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Ovarian Axis
headings.content: Normal menstruation relies on the intricate, synchronized functioning of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis, along with a responsive outflow tract. The hypothalamus secretes Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) in a pulsatile manner, which stimulates the anterior pituitary gland to synthesize and release Luteinizing Hormone (LH) and Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH). These gonadotropins act on the ovaries to promote follicular development, ovulation, and the production of sex steroids, namely estrogen and progesterone. Estrogen stimulates the proliferation of the endometrium, while progesterone induces secretory changes, preparing the uterine lining for potential implantation. If pregnancy does not occur, declining hormone levels trigger the withdrawal bleeding known as menstruation. Disruption at any level of the HPO axis—whether at the hypothalamus, pituitary, ovary, or the anatomical outflow tract—results in the cessation of menses. For nursing students, grasping this feedback loop is vital for localising the site of pathology when a patient presents with amenorrhoea.

headings.title: Classification: Primary vs. Secondary Amenorrhoea
headings.content: Amenorrhoea is classically divided into primary and secondary categories to guide differential diagnosis. Primary amenorrhoea is defined as the failure of menses to appear by age 15 in the presence of normal secondary sexual characteristics, or by age 13 if secondary sexual characteristics are entirely absent. It is frequently linked to congenital anomalies, chromosomal abnormalities (such as Turner syndrome), or anatomical defects like Müllerian agenesis. Conversely, secondary amenorrhoea is defined as the cessation of established menstruation for three consecutive cycles (or six months) in a woman who previously had normal, regular menses. The most common causes of secondary amenorrhoea include pregnancy, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disorders, and hypothalamic dysfunction related to severe weight loss, excessive exercise, or chronic stress. Differentiating between these two classifications allows healthcare providers to target investigations effectively, focusing on congenital anomalies for primary cases and acquired systemic or endocrine disruptions for secondary cases.

headings.title: Aetiology and Risk Factors
headings.content: The aetiology of amenorrhoea is diverse, encompassing anatomical, genetic, endocrine, and lifestyle factors. Common risk factors include extreme fluctuations in body weight, eating disorders like anorexia nervosa, excessive physical training (common in elite athletes), and chronic psychological stress, all of which suppress hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility. Endocrine disorders such as hyperprolactinaemia (often due to a pituitary adenoma), thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyperthyroidism), and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) are major contributors. Anatomical causes involve outflow tract obstructions, including imperforate hymen, transverse vaginal septa, or Asherman syndrome (intrauterine adhesions resulting from surgical or infectious trauma to the endometrium). Genetic and chromosomal anomalies, such as Turner syndrome (45,X) and gonadal dysgenesis, are frequent causes of primary amenorrhoea. Identifying these risk factors and underlying causes during nursing assessment is vital for formulating accurate care plans and facilitating early medical intervention.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Diagnostic Evaluation
headings.content: Clinical assessment and diagnostic evaluation of amenorrhoea require a systematic approach, beginning with a comprehensive patient history. Nurses must inquire about menstrual history, eating habits, exercise regimens, stress levels, medications, and symptoms of androgen excess or hormonal imbalance. A thorough physical examination includes measuring height, weight, Body Mass Index (BMI), and assessing for signs of hyperandrogenism (such as hirsutism and acne) or thyroid abnormalities. A baseline urine or serum pregnancy test is the mandatory first step in evaluating secondary amenorrhoea. Further diagnostic tests depend on clinical findings and may include hormonal assays (FSH, LH, TSH, prolactin, and testosterone levels), pelvic ultrasound to evaluate uterine and ovarian morphology, and genetic karyotyping for cases of primary amenorrhoea with suspected chromosomal anomalies. Hysteroscopy or imaging may be utilized if outflow tract obstruction or intrauterine scarring is suspected. Nurses play an essential role in preparing clients for these diagnostic procedures and explaining what to expect.

headings.title: Medical and Nursing Management
headings.content: Medical and nursing management of amenorrhoea focuses on treating the specific underlying cause, restoring normal menstrual function, protecting bone mineral density, and preserving future fertility where desired. Medical therapies vary widely: dopamine agonists like cabergoline are used for hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid hormone replacement for hypothyroidism, and lifestyle counseling or nutritional rehabilitation for functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea. Hormonal contraceptives or cyclic progestins are frequently prescribed to induce regular withdrawal bleeding and protect the endometrium from hyperplasia. Nursing management centers on patient advocacy, monitoring vital signs and laboratory results, administering prescribed medications safely, and educating patients on treatment adherence. Nurses also monitor for potential side effects of hormone therapies and provide holistic support. Collaborative care involving endocrinologists, gynecologists, dietitians, and mental health professionals ensures a comprehensive approach to recovery and long-term wellness.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Long-Term Implications
headings.content: Untreated amenorrhoea can lead to significant short- and long-term complications depending on the primary cause. Prolonged hypoestrogenism, commonly seen in functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea or premature ovarian insufficiency, puts women at high risk for early bone mineral density loss, leading to osteopenia and premature osteoporosis. This drastically increases the long-term risk of fragility fractures. In conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), chronic unopposed estrogen exposure without adequate progesterone-induced shedding increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma. Furthermore, chronic anovulation is a leading cause of female infertility, which can cause significant emotional and social distress, particularly in socio-cultural contexts where childbearing is heavily emphasized. Nurses must be vigilant in identifying these risks early, reinforcing adherence to medical management, and encouraging lifestyle modifications to mitigate long-term health consequences.

headings.title: Patient Education and Psychosocial Support
headings.content: Patient education and psychosocial support are vital components of comprehensive care for individuals experiencing amenorrhoea. Many patients experience anxiety, depression, a sense of body betrayal, or low self-esteem due to the loss of a key aspect of their reproductive health. In many African societies, including Nigeria, infertility or delayed menstruation carries significant cultural stigma, adding profound psychological burdens. Nurses must provide empathetic, non-judgmental counseling, validating the patient's feelings and addressing misconceptions about menstruation and fertility. Education should cover the importance of balanced nutrition, healthy weight maintenance, stress management techniques, and adherence to prescribed therapeutic regimens. Connecting patients with support groups, mental health professionals, and patient advocacy resources can greatly enhance coping mechanisms. By offering holistic, culturally sensitive care, nurses help patients navigate their diagnosis with confidence and improve their overall quality of life.
